newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries up in London, profit-taking threatens.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries up in London, profit-taking threatens.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were slightly better bid in London on Monday, but dealers said they may be vulnerable to profit-taking later following Thursday's tick up on moderate payrolls data.
The underlying tone to the market remains firm, however, with the coming week's data poised to push the long bond yield down to 6.5 percent from its current 6.62 percent, they added.
"I was a bit surprised at the strong reaction (to payrolls) on Thursday," said one trader. "There is a danger of some profit taking and I have a suspicion that could happen this afternoon."
Treasuries closed sharply higher in New York on Thursday, ahead of the Friday Independence Day holiday, after a weak employment report cut the odds of a rate hike in August.
By 0938 GMT, the 30-year cash bond was at 100-02, up from 100-01 in Tokyo and 100-00 at Thursday's New York close. Five-year paper was at 100-09, up from 100-08 in Tokyo and 100-07 in New York.
"For choice, there might be some tentative profit taking later, but it won't be anything dramatic," said Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International Europe.
"If anything, the data this week will be reasonably supportive for Treasuries."
Richardson said the overall tone in Treasuries was still bullish, and added the data-light week would do little to upset that.
He said the consumer credit data on Tuesday and June producer price data on Friday would not stand in the way of the 6.5 percent target yield on the long bond.
"We're focusing on the 6.5 percent yield at the long end now and we will probably be able to achieve that near term," he said.
The dollar was steady near its session lows against the yen by mid-morning after falling on a 129 percent rise in Japan's June trade surplus. By 1105 GMT dollar/yen stood at 112.15/25.
Richardson said the weaker currency would not have a huge impact on Treasuries.
"It's more of a yen story than a dollar story," he said, adding the market should be able to withstand the currency movements for the time being.
